articles.title: After 30 people opposed looser demolition rules for historic buildings in Saratoga Springs, New York’s mayor has paused the proposal, leaving existing protections in place while the city reviews its plans
articles.summary: Saratoga Springs Mayor John Safford has put a proposed relaxation of demolition rules for historic buildings on hold following sustained opposition from
articles.body: Saratoga Springs Mayor John Safford has put a proposed relaxation of demolition rules for historic buildings on hold following sustained opposition from residents, preservation advocates and heritage experts. The decision, announced on October 13, comes a week after a public hearing drew 30 speakers who raised concerns about the potential impact on the city’s architectural character and historic landmarks. The development was reported by the Times Union, which has covered the debate over changes to Saratoga Springs’ Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the local framework governing development and the protection of historic and architectural districts. The pause means the existing demolition safeguards will remain in place while the city considers its next steps. Safford has indicated that he is still interested in revising other parts of the development rules, including the process through which property owners can challenge decisions made by the city’s design review authorities.Why the proposal faced oppositionThe controversy centres on a plan to transfer greater authority over demolition decisions in the city’s architectural district from the Design Review Board to the City Council. Under the existing system, the board reviews demolition applications in the historic and architectural districts, with input from the Saratoga Springs Preservation Foundation where appropriate.The city’s 2022 development ordinance sets conditions that must be satisfied before a historic or architecturally significant building can be demolished. These include assessing whether the property could be adapted for another permitted use and whether efforts to find a buyer willing to preserve the structure have been unsuccessful.Critics argued that relaxing these requirements could make it easier to remove older buildings before their architectural or cultural value had been adequately considered. Some residents also warned that giving elected officials greater control over demolition decisions could introduce political considerations into the preservation process. The concerns reflect the importance of historic buildings to Saratoga Springs, a city whose identity and tourism appeal are closely associated with its architectural heritage, cultural attractions and historic streetscapes.Preservation groups welcome the pauseThe Saratoga Springs Preservation Foundation welcomed the mayor’s decision to suspend the proposed demolition-related changes in both the historic and architectural review districts. The organisation has argued for maintaining meaningful safeguards for buildings that contribute to the city’s historic character. Opposition has also extended beyond local residents. State preservation officials and the Preservation League of New York State have expressed concerns about the proposed changes, adding to pressure on the city to reconsider its approach.The debate has unfolded over several months. Since the proposal emerged in spring 2026, residents have attended public meetings and council discussions to challenge the proposed changes. The mayor had previously defended the need to revise the rules, arguing that the existing review process required greater fairness and clarity. The proposal was subsequently softened to include input from the Design Review Board, but the revisions did not resolve the concerns of preservation advocates and community members.What happens nextAlthough demolition-related amendments have been put on hold, Safford has not abandoned the broader effort to revise the development ordinance. He is still considering measures to clarify the Design Review Board’s authority and introduce an appeals process for property owners who cannot afford the cost of historically appropriate repairs to their homes.Under the proposed approach, the City Council could review aspects of the board’s procedures. The city has presented these changes as an effort to make development decisions more transparent and predictable while addressing the financial difficulties faced by some property owners.However, community organisers have cautioned that other proposed amendments may still affect historic preservation. Residents have therefore been encouraged to remain involved in the public consultation process. The next City Council public hearing is scheduled for October 20. The meeting is expected to provide another opportunity for residents and preservation advocates to express their views as Saratoga Springs considers revisions to its development rules. For now, the mayor’s decision represents a pause rather than a final resolution. The existing protections remain in force, leaving the city to weigh concerns about property rights and administrative fairness against the preservation of the historic character that helps define Saratoga Springs.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2020, a couple bought this four-bedroom English home for £465,000; after a garden landslip, it is now heading to auction with a £1 guide price while a No Occupation Order still prevents anyone living there
articles.summary: A house with four bedrooms, multiple living rooms and a private driveway would usually attract buyers looking for space and a quieter pace of life.
articles.body: A house with four bedrooms, multiple living rooms and a private driveway would usually attract buyers looking for space and a quieter pace of life. But one property in the English seaside town of St Leonards-on-Sea is being offered for less than the price of a cup of coffee. Its guide price is just £1, and the reason has little to do with the condition of the house itself. A devastating landslip destroyed its garden, leaving the property uninhabitable and its future uncertain, states an online report by Domain.From dream home to an uncertain futureAccording to Domain, the two-storey brick house was purchased by a couple in December 2020 for £465,000. With four bedrooms and approximately 126 square metres of living space, it offered the kind of room and potential that could make it a long-term family home. The owners had plans to modernise the property and make it their own. Those ambitions took a dramatic turn in February 2024, when a major landslip tore through the backyard, sending the garden more than 15 metres down a slope.The outdoor space had previously included a swimming pool, but the collapse left the area severely damaged. What had been part of the property's appeal became the source of a serious and potentially expensive problem, also states the Domain report.Why nobody can move inDespite the scale of the incident, the house itself has reportedly shown no signs of structural movement. Work has also been carried out to stabilise the garden, offering some progress towards addressing the damage, claims the online report.However, that has not been enough to make the property habitable again. A No Occupation Order remains in force, meaning nobody can legally live in the house until the outstanding issues are resolved and the necessary restrictions are lifted, states the report too.For prospective buyers, this is the central complication. Purchasing the property would not mean being able to move straight in, rent it out or immediately begin enjoying its four bedrooms and living spaces. The path towards making it usable could involve further investigations, specialist work and considerable expense. The full cost and timeline of resolving the situation remain uncertain, making the property a high-risk proposition despite its extraordinary guide price.A £1 guide price with a big catchThe owners have now decided to cut their losses and put the house up for auction with BTG Eddisons Property Auctions. It is being offered with a £1 guide price and no reserve, meaning there is no minimum sale price set by the seller. The property still has several attractive features, including a main bedroom with an ensuite bathroom, three additional bedrooms, a family bathroom, multiple reception rooms, a garage and a private driveway.Its location could also appeal to buyers willing to take on a complicated project. Situated on Foxcote, on the northern edge of St Leonards-on-Sea, the house is within a coastal town with transport connections to London and Brighton.A gamble for the right buyerThe auction is scheduled for October 29, with prospective bidders advised to conduct their own investigations before making an offer. The appeal is obvious that if the landslip-related issues can be resolved, the property could eventually regain considerable value. But the £1 starting point should not be mistaken for the total cost of ownership. For anyone considering a bid, the real questions concern the stability of the land, the requirements for lifting the No Occupation Order and the money needed to complete the necessary work.Image Courtesy: BTG Eddisons Property AuctionsReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Tibetan parliament calls China's Ladakh claims 'baseless', urges India to scrap One-China policy
articles.summary: The Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile has criticised China’s refusal to recognise Ladakh as a Union Territory of India, calling Beijing’s territorial claims
articles.body: The Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile has criticised China’s refusal to recognise Ladakh as a Union Territory of India, calling Beijing’s territorial claims baseless. It also urged New Delhi to reconsider its Tibet policy amid continuing tensions along the India-China border.The remarks come amid a diplomatic exchange between New Delhi and Beijing over India’s decision to standardise the names of 28 geographical locations and features in Ladakh on official maps, prompting China to reiterate its objections to India’s territorial claims.According to news agency ANI, Dolma Tsering, speaker of the Tibetan Parliament-in-Exile, said China’s attempts to rename geographical locations in Tibet and build villages along border areas were developments India should take seriously in its diplomatic engagement with Beijing.“Beijing’s repeated attempts to rename geographical locations in Tibet and its construction of villages along border areas were concerning developments that India should take seriously while engaging diplomatically with China,” she said.Tsering also cautioned against allowing economic engagement to take precedence over security concerns, saying, “India should not allow trade and business engagements to take precedence over border security, stressing that both issues must be addressed together.”She argued that China’s territorial claims required historical evidence and maintained that Tibet remained central to the unresolved boundary dispute. “A lasting resolution to the border dispute would be difficult without addressing the Tibet issue,” she said.Tsering further alleged that China’s policies promoting ethnic assimilation and prioritising Mandarin over Tibetan threatened Tibet’s distinct cultural and religious identity.She reiterated that the Tibetan leadership’s Middle Way Approach sought a negotiated settlement that would allow Tibetans to preserve their culture, identity and faith, and urged Beijing to resume dialogue.Tibetan MP Gompo Dhondup also rejected China’s claims over Ladakh and other Himalayan regions, including Arunachal Pradesh, asserting that these territories were integral to India and that Beijing had no right to interfere in India’s sovereignty.Dhondup argued that a free and independent Tibet could serve as a peaceful buffer between India and China along their more than 3,000-kilometre border. He called on New Delhi to reconsider its position on Tibet and repeal its One-China policy, saying stronger support for Tibet would serve both Tibetan aspirations and India’s security interests.India rejects China’s objections over LadakhThe latest remarks follow India’s response to Beijing’s objections to the naming exercise. On Tuesday, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal reiterated India’s position that Ladakh was an integral part of the country.“It is reiterated that the UT of Ladakh is an integral and inalienable part of India. No amount of denial by the Chinese side can change this established fact,” Jaiswal said.The exchange followed a notification by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) standardising names for 28 locations and geographical features in Ladakh on official Survey of India maps, including Gogra and Hot Spring, sites associated with the 2020 military standoff.Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning opposed the move, saying Beijing had never recognised the territory as Indian. “The move is illegal and invalid and cannot change the fact that the relevant areas in the western sector of the China-India boundary have always belonged to China,” she said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Russia hits Coca-Cola, McDonald's sites in Ukraine but Donald Trump staying silent
articles.summary: Russian attacks on American businesses operating in Ukraine have damaged facilities linked to Coca-Cola, McDonald’s and PepsiCo in recent months, raising
articles.body: Russian attacks on American businesses operating in Ukraine have damaged facilities linked to Coca-Cola, McDonald’s and PepsiCo in recent months, raising questions about why the Donald Trump administration has been more vocal in criticising Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure than in condemning attacks on US companies.The attacks have hit factories and warehouses, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy describing a drone strike on a Coca-Cola plant near Kyiv in early September as a “clear signal” to Washington.Andy Hunder, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Ukraine, said Russian missiles and drones had damaged facilities belonging to some of the biggest American brands. He told CNN that while Russia had targeted US businesses before, the scale of the attacks in recent months was unprecedented.“This is a direct hit with drones and missiles, and they keep hitting them. It’s sending a message that they’re targeting American business. We’re not seeing any response from the White House,” he said.Coca-Cola plant, McDonald’s warehouse targetedA Russian drone struck a Coca-Cola factory outside Kyiv in early September. On September 3, Zelenskyy referred to the attack in his nightly video address, saying, “Today, the Russians struck a Coca-Cola plant with a drone. Coca-Cola has become such an enemy to them that they’re burning it down with their Shaheds,” referring to “Iranian-designed drones.”“This is a clear signal from Russia to America. The Russians cannot possibly be unaware that this is an American enterprise,” Zelenskyy added.Later in September, a Russian attack drone hit a warehouse used by McDonald’s in the Kyiv region. Zelenskyy said the strike destroyed the warehouse, while McDonald’s Ukraine confirmed that “a warehouse operated by one of our logistics partners in the Kyiv region was damaged in a drone attack on 25 September.”“An attack drone – against ordinary food products,” Zelenskyy wrote on X. “The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centers, internet providers – for Russia, ordinary life in and of itself is simply a target.”The damage has affected operations at McDonald’s restaurants in Ukraine, which are now offering a reduced menu. PepsiCo also confirmed in late August that a production facility in the Mykolaiv region had been damaged, although no casualties were reported.Hunder said the attacks were hitting American investors and commercial interests directly.“We need this to stop because these are American interests, American money, American investors that are being hit and are being targeted,” he said.US response under scrutinyThe lack of a strong public response from the Trump administration has drawn criticism from some US lawmakers, including Democrats who have urged the White House to do more to protect American businesses in Ukraine and condemn Moscow’s actions.However, companies operating in the country have differed over whether to speak publicly about the attacks. A former senior State Department official told CNN that some businesses were reluctant to disclose that their facilities had been targeted repeatedly.“Some businesses do want us to raise this,” Hunder said, adding that others “are treading very carefully.”The American Chamber of Commerce has raised the issue with visiting US lawmakers from both parties and asked them to bring it to the White House. Hunder said the organisation had also sought a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner last month to discuss the condition of American businesses in Ukraine, including the latest attacks. “We didn’t get any response on that,” he said.A White House official said Trump wanted the war to end and that his administration remained committed to efforts to secure peace.“The president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done,” the official said, arguing that the US is “the only country in the world” that can “play a constructive role in speaking to both sides in working towards bringing the war to an end.”Trump had publicly expressed displeasure after a Russian strike on a US electronics factory in August 2025, saying he had told Russian President Vladimir Putin that he was “not happy about it”.Contrast with pressure on KyivThe administration’s response to attacks on American businesses contrasts with its pressure on Ukraine to stop striking Russian energy facilities. Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure for rising fuel prices, which have also been driven up by the US-Iran war.CNN reported in February that the administration had warned Kyiv that strikes on a Russian Black Sea oil facility late last year had affected US investments in Kazakhstan. In recent weeks, the US has also threatened to restrict intelligence sharing and ammunition supplies to Ukraine if it continues attacking Russian energy infrastructure, according to sources cited by CNN.Last Friday, Trump announced a deal to waive sanctions and purchase diesel from Russia, despite US law. Hunder said he struggled to understand the administration’s relative silence on attacks against American companies, particularly given its stated support for US businesses.“Any company, any business, wants to have some sort of protection. You would expect your government to stand up in your corner and fight the fight with you, especially if it’s a foreign military that is attacking the American companies,” he said.The former State Department official told CNN that officials in Washington often believe Ukraine-related discussions should be handled by Witkoff and Kushner, making it difficult for others to draw attention to the attacks.“The idea that you would get a rationale back” on why the US was silent about the attacks “is not something that people can expect,” they said.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2026, engineers made an epoxy composite with sterilised post-consumer diaper fibres; at 25% fibre, flexural strength rose 1,303% and tensile strength about 88% over the plain resin
articles.summary: Discover the innovative 2026 study that reveals how sterilized post-consumer diaper fibers can significantly enhance the strength of epoxy composites, providing a sustainable solution for municipal solid waste management.
articles.body: Disposable nappies address an issue for parents and create a problem for cities. A nappy is a tidy sandwich of cellulose fibre, plastic sheets and a gel that absorbs fluids, and it is thrown away after one use. Most of it goes to landfill or an incinerator. It is tough to separate the layers and the waste is, to put it mildly, unpleasant to manage.Existing recycling projects show that disposable nappies contain several recoverable materials. The European Commission explains that disposable nappies mainly contain cellulose fibres, polyolefin plastics and superabsorbent polymer. In that project, the items are opened, sterilised by means of steam in a rotary autoclave, dried and divided into components by mechanical and optical separators. A separate study published in 2026 examined whether fibres recovered from sterilised nappy waste could reinforce epoxy resin.What the study showedPublished in Results in Engineering in June 2026, the paper Development and characterisation of post-consumer diaper waste reinforced epoxy composite: A circular economy approach to municipal solid waste management examines the use of sterilised diaper waste as reinforcement in epoxy resin. Epoxy is a rigid thermosetting resin used in adhesives, coatings, and composite materials. On its own, epoxy can be strong but brittle, so engineers often reinforce it with fibres to improve its mechanical performance.The researchers developed composites from sterilised post-consumer diaper fibres, according to the statistics presented in the study. At a 25% fibre content by weight, the composite's flexural strength rose from 2.08 MPa for the plain resin to 29.2 MPa, an increase of about 1,303%. Tensile strength rose from 13.1 MPa to 24.6 MPa, an increase of approximately 88%, according to the study. Flexural strength is a measure of how much the material resists bending. Tensile strength is the measure of how much the material resists being ripped apart.Those are remarkable numbers and they ought to be read carefully. What is more, a very significant percentage increase might start from a low foundation; thus the absolute strength numbers count as much as the headline percentage. Again, the result is from laboratory samples, not from a finished product tested in service. A reasonable summation would be that diaper fibre does seem to perform as a reinforcement in this system, and that more testing would be needed before anyone makes anything load-bearing out of it.Why the waste is worth the troubleThat breakdown shows why a composite maker might care. The European Union's EMBRACED project identifies used nappies, incontinence products and other absorbent hygiene products as a substantial waste stream that can be processed to recover cellulose and plastics. It reports that around 900,000 tonnes of this waste are incinerated or landfilled in Italy every year, 8.5 million tonnes in Europe and more than 30 million tonnes worldwide. The European Commission reports that Europe generates about 8.5 million tonnes of absorbent hygiene product waste each year, much of which has traditionally been sent to landfill or incineration. The EMBRACED process opens and steam-sterilises the waste, dries it and separates its recoverable components for further use. That breakdown shows why a composite maker might care. Cellulose fibre is the largest recoverable fraction, and fibre is exactly what a composite needs. A route that turns the fibre into a stronger epoxy would give recyclers a use for a material stream that currently has few buyers.Other routes, and the open questionsEpoxy composites are not the only idea on the table. In December 2025, BASF announced a pilot with Essity and TU Wien in which diaper waste was gasified at temperatures above 600 degrees Celsius.The pilot used gasification at temperatures above 600°C to convert the waste into a gas mixture containing carbon monoxide and hydrogen, which can serve as feedstock for chemical production. BASF said the process could handle used nappies and other absorbent hygiene products without complex pretreatment. Gasification breaks the waste down to its chemical building blocks, while the epoxy route keeps the fibre intact and puts it to work as a reinforcement.Any diaper-based composite has to answer some practical questions. Cellulose absorbs water, and moisture can weaken fibre-reinforced plastics over time. Collection has to deliver diapers separately from other rubbish, and sterilisation has to be reliable every time. Cost also matters, because epoxy producers will only use a recycled filler if it is consistent and cheaper or better than what they already buy. In short, a 2026 study reports that sterilised diaper fibre can strengthen epoxy, with the biggest gains at 25 per cent fibre content. It is early laboratory work, but it points to a possible second life for one of the most stubborn items in household waste.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Farmers rely on tall fescue across 35 million US acres for hardy pasture; a fungus inside much of the grass now costs the beef industry about $1 billion a year
articles.summary: Explore how tall fescue, a popular grass on 35 million acres of U.S. pastureland, provides resilience against harsh conditions but harbors a toxic fungus that costs the beef industry $1 billion annually. Learn about potential solutions to mitigate fescue toxicosis.
articles.body: Tall fescue grows across more than 35 million acres of US pasture and hayland and is valued for its ability to survive drought, tolerate grazing and grow on difficult soils, but microscopic fungus living inside many tall fescue plants produces toxins that are associated with an estimated $1 billion in annual lost production for the US beef industry, according to the US Department of Agriculture’s Agricultural Research Service (USDA ARS). The agency describes the condition as fescue toxicosis, a livestock disorder linked to toxic compounds produced by the fungus.The fungus helps the grass surviveTall fescue is a cool-season perennial grass that is widely used across the eastern and southeastern United States; it establishes readily, forms dense pasture cover and can remain productive on land where other forage grasses struggle. Farmers also value its ability to tolerate grazing pressure and retain usable growth into cooler months.The fungus is called Epichloë coenophiala, and lives between the plant’s cells. Its relationship with tall fescue is mutually beneficial, in a sense that the grass supplies the fungus with nutrients and a place to live, while fungal compounds help the plant withstand environmental stress and deter certain pests. The problem comes from a group of chemicals called ergot alkaloids, since one of the principal compounds, ergovaline, can constrict blood vessels in animals that consume infected forage. Virginia Tech’s agricultural extension specialists explain that the fungus does not usually change the plant’s outward appearance, so farmers cannot reliably identify toxic plants by sight alone.Cattle can eat the grass but gain less weightAnimals may eat less, gain weight more slowly, develop elevated body temperatures and spend more time standing in shade or water during hot weather, while reproductive performance and milk production can also decline. The effects can become especially difficult to manage during summer, since ergot alkaloids restrict blood flow, which makes it harder for cattle to release body heat. Animals may reduce their feed intake and grazing time, while producers see lower weight gains than expected from an otherwise productive pasture.Cattle can develop fescue foot in more severe cases, which is a condition that is associated with reduced circulation to the extremities, and the resulting tissue damage can affect hooves, ears and tails. The symptoms vary with exposure, animal sensitivity and environmental conditions, so not every animal grazing infected pasture will show the same signs. The economic estimate covers lost production rather than a single disease-treatment bill, since lower weight gains, reproductive losses and other performance problems can affect returns across a beef operation.Removing the fungus created another problemEarly efforts to address the issue focused on tall fescue varieties without the fungal endophyte, and those plants avoided the toxin problem, but they often lacked the persistence and stress tolerance that made traditional tall fescue so useful. Researchers later developed varieties that contained selected, or “novel,” endophytes that retain many of the grass’s agronomic advantages without producing the same harmful levels of ergot alkaloids.Producers can also manage existing infected fields through grazing decisions and alternative forage crops, and the appropriate approach depends on pasture condition, climate, available land and the cost of reseeding. It is expensive to replace an established pasture, and poorly adapted alternatives may not persist as well.Red clover offers another management optionUSDA researchers have also studied interseeding red clover into infected tall fescue pasture, and in a two-season grazing experiment, Angus-cross steers grazing pastures containing red clover recorded higher average daily gains than cattle on tall fescue alone. Researchers attributed some of the benefit to isoflavones in legumes, which can help counteract the blood-vessel constriction that is associated with ergot alkaloids.The study provides evidence for one management strategy that may reduce some adverse effects while farmers continue to use established grass stands. Tall fescue remains useful because it is hardy and productive, and the challenge for producers is to preserve those advantages without exposing cattle to the toxic effects of the fungus living inside the grass.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2009, Barack Obama faced years of stalled land bills; he signed the Public Lands Act, and more than 2 million wilderness acres and 1,000 river miles were protected
articles.summary: In 2009, President Barack Obama signed the Omnibus Public Land Management Act, protecting over 2 million acres of wilderness and more than 1,000 river miles. This significant legislation marked a major advancement in federal conservation efforts in the United States.
articles.body: For years, efforts to protect some of America’s most treasured landscapes had struggled in Congress. Conservationists, local communities and lawmakers had pushed for stronger safeguards for wilderness areas and rivers, but progress remained slow as individual proposals stalled. In 2009, lawmakers bundled many of those long-pending conservation measures into one bill.According to the US Department of the Interior, Barack Obama signed the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009 on 30 March, less than 100 days into his presidency. The legislation added more than two million acres across nine states to the National Wilderness Preservation System and designated over 1,000 miles of rivers. It also strengthened the framework for managing millions of acres of conservation lands, marking an important step in federal efforts to safeguard wildlife habitats, free-flowing waterways and landscapes.Years of stalled bills finally led to a breakthroughThe US Department of the Interior also states that the act grew out of decades-long efforts to expand protection for the nation’s public lands. Across the country, conservationists had tried to protect wilderness areas and rivers from development, but individual proposals often stalled in Congress. Bundling the proposals into one legislative package created an opportunity to advance several measures at once.The bill was one of the most significant federal conservation measures in years. Interior Secretary Ken Salazar noted that the passage of the bill involved many years of hard work, and he paid tribute to the citizens, the tribal leadership, local politicians, business people, and representatives from both sides of the aisle for their part in making this happen. President Obama signed the bill into law as Public Law 111-11. Obama’s signing statement said that the act would conserve millions of acres of federal land, protect over a thousand miles of rivers, and create thousands of miles of trails.Two million acres and a thousand miles of riversAmong the act’s major accomplishments was the addition of more than two million acres across nine states to the National Wilderness Preservation System. Signed by President Barack Obama, the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009 brought together numerous conservation measures, including the designation of new wilderness areas. These included Mount Hood in Oregon, areas around Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado, and lands near Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore in Michigan, along with wilderness areas in Utah. However, these designations did not mean that the entirety of each named national park or protected landscape became wilderness. The act also protected forests, mountains and desert landscapes across the country. By granting these areas wilderness status, the law strengthened safeguards against development and other activities incompatible with wilderness protection, helping conserve habitats, preserve natural landscapes and maintain opportunities for low-impact recreation.A lasting framework for conservationAccording to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009 gave the Bureau of Land Management’s National Landscape Conservation System permanent legal status. The system brought together nationally significant landscapes, including national monuments, national conservation areas, wilderness areas, scenic rivers and historic trails, under a common conservation framework. The study also explains that these classifications provided different levels of protection, ranging from largely undisturbed natural environments to areas with recreational and educational facilities. This framework helped establish a lasting basis for conserving ecological and cultural resources.The act also covered national parks, historic sites, trails, groundwater, oceans and water resources. It included provisions for establishing conservation areas and restoring public lands, reflecting a broader approach to protecting landscapes, rivers and wildlife. Although the legislation did not resolve every environmental challenge in the United States, President Barack Obama’s signing of the act on 30 March 2009 marked a significant step in federal land protection. By bringing together numerous conservation measures, the law secured protection for millions of acres of wilderness and more than a thousand miles of rivers. Its passage also demonstrated how public advocacy and bipartisan cooperation could translate conservation priorities into federal law.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A Rhode Island family planned more than 200 affordable apartments on 31 acres; the town seized the site for a municipal complex after a $775,000 appraisal, but a federal judge later voided the taking
articles.summary: A federal judge has blocked the Town of Johnston, Rhode Island, from taking control of a 31-acre property planned for affordable housing.
articles.body: A federal judge has blocked the Town of Johnston, Rhode Island, from taking control of a 31-acre property planned for affordable housing. The judge ruled that town officials did not have the legal authority to seize the land. US District Judge Melissa R. DuBose overturned the town's decision to take the property near George Waterman Road. The ruling clears the way for the Santoro family and their development company, SCLS Realty LLC, to continue plans for a 252-unit housing complex. The decision ends a major legal dispute between town officials and property developers over land rights, local zoning rules and state requirements for affordable housing.Secret condemnation and social media discoveryThe dispute began when the Santoro family submitted plans to build a large residential development on their 31-acre property. Under Rhode Island law, developers can avoid certain local zoning restrictions if a town has less than 10 per cent of its housing classified as affordable. Johnston's affordable housing share stood at about 7.9 per cent. To stop the proposed development, the town government, led by Mayor Joseph Polisena Jr., moved to take the property through eminent domain. This legal power allows governments to acquire private land for public use under certain conditions. Town officials said the land was needed for a combined municipal complex that would include a new police headquarters, fire department headquarters and town hall. In early 2025, the town filed the condemnation paperwork, deposited an appraisal amount of $775,000 in a state court registry and transferred the property's title to the municipality. According to legal filings in SCLS Realty, LLC v. Town of Johnston, documented in court records and reported by the Washington Examiner, town officials completed the transfer without notifying the owners beforehand. The Santoro family learned that the property had been seized only after seeing an announcement posted by town officials on social media.Legal action and constitutional challengeIn March 2025, SCLS Realty LLC filed a federal lawsuit against the town. The company was represented by the Pacific Legal Foundation and local legal counsel. It argued that the seizure was unconstitutional and amounted to an unlawful taking of private property. According to reports by Rhode Island Current and The Public's Radio, the lawsuit accused the town of creating its own condemnation process, breaking open meeting laws and claiming a public purpose to delay the housing project. The Pacific Legal Foundation criticised the move as a "sham taking". The organisation argued that town officials had used their eminent domain powers to get around Rhode Island's affordable housing requirements. Mayor Joseph Polisena Jr. rejected claims that the town had acted in bad faith. Speaking to local media, he said the planned municipal complex was the main reason for the land acquisition. "No, it's about building the complex," Polisena Jr. told The Public's Radio. "I mean, that is the number one priority. I don't think there's anything more quintessential to a municipal government than providing public safety." The Rhode Island Attorney General's office later reviewed the town's initial actions and found that the town council had violated the state's Open Meetings Act during its early votes on the land acquisition. The council held another vote in March 2025 to approve the condemnation again. However, the developers continued with their federal lawsuit, seeking to overturn the seizure altogether.Court strikes down municipal overreachIn a ruling issued by the US District Court for the District of Rhode Island, Judge Melissa R. DuBose sided with the developers and declared the town's seizure of the property invalid from the beginning. The court found that Johnston officials had failed to follow the legal procedures required to use eminent domain. Judge DuBose ruled that local governments cannot create their own condemnation systems to avoid the legal protections that apply when private property is taken. The decision prevents the town from relying on the invalidated process to take control of the land. "This ruling reins in the Town's obvious abuse of power and protects every American whose land a government might decide it wants," said Kady Valois, an attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, in a statement released after the court's decision.Impact on local housing mandatesThe court's ruling restores ownership of the 31-acre property to SCLS Realty LLC, allowing the Santoro family to move forward with its plans for the 252-unit housing development. The decision could have wider effects across Rhode Island, where several towns have struggled to meet the state's requirement that at least 10 per cent of their housing stock be affordable. Legal experts working on land-use issues say the ruling shows that local councils cannot use land seizures to avoid state-backed housing requirements. Johnston officials indicated after the ruling that they might consider other legal options concerning the property. However, the federal court's order prevents the town from interfering with the site through the eminent domain proceedings that have been declared invalid. The future of the proposed housing complex will now depend on the next steps taken by the developers and any further lawful action pursued by the town.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 2002, Japan widened a 70-metre road using crushed oyster shells in its base; testing found the shell section exceeded the ground improvement target
articles.summary: Discover how Japan transformed seafood waste into a sustainable solution for road strengthening, showcasing positive results from a unique 2002 engineering experiment with crushed oyster shells.
articles.body: Discarded oyster shells are often associated with seafood waste, stockpiles and the challenge of finding storage space. In parts of Japan, oyster-farming shells became the focus of a practical engineering experiment. Rather than sending the material for disposal or using it only in agriculture, researchers investigated whether crushed shells could help strengthen the ground beneath roads.According to a study published in the Journal of the Society of Materials Science, Japan, crushed oyster shells were tested in a Japanese road-widening project in March 2002, with the trial covering a 70-metre stretch. Researchers monitored the road’s response to traffic using pavement deflection measurements and found that deflection decreased over time. The section containing nearly dry oyster shells also achieved an estimated California Bearing Ratio above the target set for ground improvement. The findings suggest that discarded oyster shells may be useful for strengthening road subgrades, although further testing is needed under different conditions.Why Japan was looking for a use for discarded oyster shellsThe experiment aimed to address a practical problem in oyster-producing areas. After oysters were removed, the shells would pile up in storage yards. Some of these would be used again as an additive to animal feeds, fertilisers, and soil conditioners. This method of using shells did not always keep up with production levels. Piling up shells caused problems in terms of occupying space and creating foul odours and worsening the environment. Using these shells for crushing purposes presented an alternate solution. The crushed shells would be used for making better roads.The approach was not entirely untested. A study published in Doboku Gakkai Ronbunshu in September 2002 examined the suitability of crushed oyster shells for road subgrades through laboratory experiments and simulated ground-improvement tests. The researchers found that incorporating roughly 20% crushed shells could improve the ability of construction equipment to travel over the treated ground and could contribute to the effectiveness of soil stabilisation. The study suggested that the small, irregular shell fragments could perform well beneath asphalt pavements. The next experiment moved the research outside the confines of the laboratory. Rather than depend only on the results of laboratory testing on samples, the engineers were able to see the performance of the material after the road had been built.What happened after vehicles began using the road?The researchers used a falling weight deflectometer to measure how much the road surface bent under a controlled load, helping them assess the pavement’s strength without digging into it. The Society of Materials Science, Japan also reports that maximum deflection at the loading point tended to decrease during the monitoring period, suggesting the pavement resisted bending more effectively under the test conditions. The best results came from the section containing nearly dried oyster-shell fragments, where the estimated California Bearing Ratio (CBR), a measure of soil strength and resistance to penetration, exceeded the target set for ground improvement.These findings suggested that oyster-shell fragments could be a useful alternative in the road-widening project, but they did not establish that shell powder or other forms of oyster-shell material could replace conventional road materials in every situation. Further testing under different soil and weather conditions, along with longer-term monitoring, would be needed to determine how well the material performed over time.Could seafood waste become a regular road material?The significance of the Japanese study lay in its practical approach to waste management. Rather than sending discarded oyster shells for disposal, the researchers tested whether the material could serve a useful purpose in road construction. The 70-metre trial produced encouraging results for the ground supporting the pavement, but it did not establish that oyster shells could be used directly as a road-surfacing material. The study also did not quantify the long-term cost savings or establish how the material would perform under different conditions over many years. Nevertheless, it showed that locally available shell waste could meet a specific ground-improvement target under the conditions tested.The March 2002 project provided a field-based assessment of oyster-shell fragments as a construction material, moving beyond the idea of waste reuse to examine their performance under real road conditions. Its findings offered evidence for a potential use in areas with substantial quantities of discarded shells, while leaving questions about durability, wider applications and long-term economic benefits unresolved.You use AI every day. articles.title: In Cameroon’s black-cotton-soil road experiment, researchers mixed bamboo charcoal, quarry dust and lime into the ground; its bearing score rose from 2.7% with bamboo charcoal alone to 19% with the final mixture
articles.summary: Discover how researchers in Cameroon have combined bamboo charcoal, quarry dust, and lime to significantly enhance the load-bearing capacity of Black Cotton Soil, paving the way for durable roads in challenging conditions.
articles.body: Building durable roads on weak soil is costly, particularly in regions where the ground swells when wet and shrinks as it dries. In Cameroon, researchers tested whether bamboo charcoal, quarry dust and lime could strengthen Black Cotton Soil, an expansive soil that can weaken road foundations.According to a study published in the International Journal of Civil Engineering, the researchers examined how combining the three materials affected the soil’s load-bearing capacity. The best-performing mixture, containing 20% bamboo charcoal, 12% quarry dust and 5% lime, increased the soaked California Bearing Ratio (CBR) from 2.7% to 19%. The laboratory results suggested that the combination could improve the suitability of this difficult soil for road construction, although its performance under actual road conditions would require further assessment.Why Black Cotton Soil creates problems for roadsBlack Cotton Soil contains large amounts of clay and changes volume as moisture levels vary. In wet seasons, Black Cotton Soil absorbs moisture and swells. When it dries, it tends to shrink and form cracks. These changes can strain road foundations and deform the road surface. The problem is especially serious when the subgrade, the prepared earth beneath the road, is made of Black Cotton Soil.The research explains that bamboo charcoal was first used as a soil amendment to alter the soil’s engineering properties. The researchers tested several charcoal proportions and selected the 20% bamboo charcoal mix for further analysis. The selected mixture achieved only a 2.7% soaked CBR. That led the researchers to test other substances that could improve the mixture. Lime and quarry dust were added in sequence to enable the scientists to observe the impact of each substance on the bearing capacity of the soil. This approach matters because soil stabilisation involves more than simply adding one material to the soil.How quarry dust and lime improved the mixtureQuarry dust is a fine material produced during rock crushing. When added to the bamboo-charcoal-treated soil, it helped improve the mixture’s bearing capacity. The addition of lime produced a further increase, bringing the soaked CBR to 19%, more than seven times the value recorded for the charcoal-only mixture. The researchers also found that the soil’s Plasticity Index fell to 11.2%, indicating a reduction in its plasticity.These results are consistent with other studies on stabilising expansive soils. A study published in Construction Materials found that chemically stabilising black cotton soil improved its engineering properties, highlighting the importance of selecting suitable additives. However, the Cameroon experiment’s results came from laboratory tests and do not guarantee the same performance on construction sites, where soil composition, drainage, rainfall and compaction can vary. Further field testing would be needed to establish how reliably the mixture performs under real road conditions.Could the mixture be used in road construction?The Cameroon experiment was notable for combining three materials to improve the strength of difficult soil. Bamboo charcoal offered a potential use for processed bamboo, while quarry dust provided a way to reuse a by-product of stone processing. Lime, already used in soil stabilisation to modify plasticity and improve soil properties, formed the third part of the mixture. The significance lay in testing how these materials worked together, rather than assuming that any one additive could deliver the same results on its own.For road builders, the approach could be useful in areas where expansive soils are common and conventional ground improvement is expensive. However, its practical value would depend on the cost of producing and transporting bamboo charcoal, the local availability of quarry dust and the amount of lime required. The environmental impact of charcoal production would also need to be considered.Further field trials would be necessary to establish how the treated soil responded to repeated traffic loads, wet and dry cycles and changing groundwater levels, as well as whether the mixture could be prepared and compacted consistently at construction sites. Although the researchers reported a substantial increase in bearing capacity under the tested conditions, its performance and cost-effectiveness in wider road-building applications would require further assessment.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mike Tyson and wife Lakiha sued in £1.5 million High Court battle over Rabona sponsorship deal after alleged refusal to film giant talking pigeon video; boxer denies breach of contract
articles.summary: Mike Tyson and his wife, Lakiha Tyson, are embroiled in a £1.5 million High Court legal battle in London over claims that the former heavyweight boxing
articles.body: Mike Tyson and his wife, Lakiha Tyson, are embroiled in a £1.5 million High Court legal battle in London over claims that the former heavyweight boxing champion unlawfully withdrew from a lucrative marketing campaign after objecting to a promotional video featuring a giant talking pigeon. According to a report by The Independent, Medier Ltd, the company behind online gambling brand Rabona, is suing Tyson and his promotional business, Tyrannic, alleging breach of a sponsorship agreement signed in January 2024. Tyson and Tyrannic deny the allegations.The dispute centres on an agreement under which Tyson was to promote Rabona’s gaming services through live-streaming events and other promotional activities. The contract reportedly involved a $2 million fee, payable to Tyrannic in instalments, of which nearly $190,000 was paid before the relationship broke down.As reported by The Independent, Medier alleges that Tyson and Tyrannic failed to participate in agreed live-streaming events and terminated the contract without proper notice.Barrister Ali Reza Sinai, representing Medier, told the court that Tyson and his company effectively walked away from the agreement after he secured a much more lucrative deal to fight YouTuber-turned-boxer Jake Paul.Describing the Netflix-backed exhibition bout as the “elephant in the room”, Sinai argued that Tyson and Tyrannic had lost interest in the Rabona arrangement once the fight was confirmed.“The defendants simply lost interest in the service agreement once the more rewarding exhibition fight was firmly agreed,” Sinai said in written submissions. He also argued that fulfilling the sponsorship obligations had become inconvenient for Tyson and his company.Giant talking pigeon at centre of legal disputeAt the heart of the disagreement is a proposed promotional video called ‘Talking Pigeons’, which Tyson’s legal team says went well beyond what had been agreed under the sponsorship contract.According to the court submissions detailed by The Independent, the concept required Tyson to interact with four presenters, including one dressed as a giant pigeon. The boxer was allegedly expected to participate in scripted role-play, answer questions, share childhood stories and teach the presenters how to box.The proposed segment also involved a mannequin bearing the face of Tyson’s former opponent, Evander Holyfield, which the presenters were expected to punch. Tyson would then play casino games on the Rabona website while interacting with them through a video link.Medier’s legal team maintains that Tyson and Tyrannic failed to honour their contractual commitments. The defence, however, argues that the proposed entertainment format was never part of the performance Tyson had agreed to provide.Tyson’s lawyers say promotional demands exceeded contractBarrister Amanda Hadkiss, representing Tyson and Tyrannic, told the court that the requested performance went “far beyond the scope of what might reasonably be considered to have even been required” under the agreement.She argued that the contract limited Tyson’s filmed activities to playing casino games, including slots, poker and roulette, or participating in other games and events featured on Rabona’s website, provided those activities had been approved.The defence contends that the ‘Talking Pigeons’ concept was fundamentally different from the activities specified in the contract.Hadkiss said Tyson was not contractually required to take part in the proposed show and argued that Tyrannic had therefore not breached the agreement by indicating in advance that he would not attend or by his subsequent non-attendance.The High Court will have to consider the competing interpretations of the sponsorship agreement as the hearing continues.Jake Paul fight and Amsterdam event add to disputeThe court heard that Tyson’s exhibition bout against Jake Paul was initially scheduled for July 20, 2024, although it eventually took place in November that year. Tyson lost the contest, which was streamed on Netflix.Under the Rabona agreement, Tyson was also expected to attend a promotional event at a major gambling conference in Amsterdam scheduled for July 16 to 19, 2024.Medier’s barrister argued that Tyson and Tyrannic may have been concerned that the Amsterdam appearance could conflict with restrictions under the Netflix agreement, which allegedly limited non-fight-related sponsorship activities during the build-up to the bout.Sinai argued that there was a “clear and significant risk” that the defendants could be viewed as breaching the Netflix agreement if the Amsterdam sponsorship event was advertised and went ahead.The defence disputes that Tyson’s withdrawal amounted to a contractual breach, maintaining that the nature of the requested promotional performance itself exceeded the agreed obligations.Mike Tyson’s lifelong love of pigeonsThe dispute has an unusual connection to one of Tyson’s best-known personal interests: his lifelong affection for racing pigeons.As noted in The Independent’s report, Tyson has frequently spoken about his love for the birds and their importance during his difficult childhood in New York. In his autobiography, he wrote about how caring for pigeons became a meaningful part of his early life.He has also recounted an incident in which a man killed one of his pet pigeons, an experience he has linked to his first involvement in physical confrontation.Tyson became the youngest heavyweight world champion in boxing history in 1986, at the age of 20. Known for his explosive power and aggressive fighting style, he later retired with a professional record of 50 victories and seven defeats.The current dispute is not about Tyson’s affection for pigeons itself, but about whether the proposed pigeon-themed promotional show fell within the obligations he had accepted under the Rabona agreement.The High Court hearing is continuing. No finding of liability has been made against Tyson or Tyrannic.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Najmeh Amini, a 23-year-old Iranian accounting student, faces a death sentence for alleged blasphemy linked to a social media post. The case highlights the Iranian government's crackdown on dissent following nationwide protests.
articles.body: An Iranian accounting student has been sentenced to death on blasphemy charges over a social media post.Najmeh Amini, 23, is being held at Vakilabad prison in Mashhad, north-eastern Iran. She has received a death sentence in one case and a prison term of 12 years, six months and one day in another, according to The Guardian.The case comes amid a wider crackdown following nationwide protests in January, during which thousands of people were reportedly killed. According to the HRAI news agency, Hrana, said more than 50,000 people were arrested during the crackdown.What are the charges against Najmeh Amini?A source close to Amini’s family told the US-based Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRAI) that she was sentenced to death on a charge of sab ol-nabi, as cited by The Guardian.Amini was reportedly arrested after Iran’s Cyber Police, known as Fata, monitored her online activity. The specific content of the social media post has not been made public.In a separate case, she was sentenced to 12 years, six months and one day in prison on charges including acting against national security and spreading propaganda against the government.Iranian newspaper Khorasan, which confirmed the judicial proceedings, reported that Amini told the court she had made the remarks while hallucinating after taking psychedelic mushrooms with friends. Her defence described the incident as a “slip of the tongue”.The presiding judge reportedly rejected the explanation, questioning why Amini had not insulted other individuals or opponents of the Iranian government while in the same state.Under Article 262 of Iran’s Islamic Penal Code, insulting the Prophet Muhammad or revered Shia figures is punishable by death. Article 263 provides exemptions in certain circumstances, including where the remarks were made without deliberate intent.What did Amini say in her appeal for help?An audio recording attributed to Amini and released last month contains an appeal for international intervention. She called on the United Nations, lawyers and human rights organisations to investigate her case.“I do not want to make a hero out of myself today. I only want one thing: be my voice,” she said.In the recording, Amini also spoke about her hopes for the future and the distress her situation had caused her family.“I am an innocent young girl with so many hopes and dreams,” she said, adding that her parents were waiting for her and feared losing her.Her appeal has added a personal dimension to concerns raised by rights groups over the death sentence and its implications for online expression in Iran.Why are human rights groups concerned?Rights organisations have warned that Iranian authorities are increasingly using executions to intimidate the public and suppress dissent.Norway-based Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO) reported that more than 600 executions had already been carried out in Iran this year.Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, the organisation’s director, said Amini’s sentence risked extending the use of capital punishment to peaceful expression. He also warned that the Iranian authorities were testing how far the international community would tolerate such cases.Death sentences for blasphemy remain relatively uncommon in Iran despite the recent rise in executions. The last documented executions in blasphemy-related cases took place on May 8, 2023, when Yousef Mehrad and Sadrollah Fazeli-Zare were executed after convictions linked to social media activity.You use AI every day. articles.title: US needs 1.7 million skilled workers a year, but Trump's visa crackdown could leave industries short
articles.summary: The US needs roughly 1.7 million new skilled workers annually through 2035, according to The State of America’s Skilled Trades report.
articles.body: The US needs roughly 1.7 million new skilled workers annually through 2035, according to The State of America’s Skilled Trades report. Yet the Trump administration has tightened restrictions on foreign workers, including suspending eight technology and outsourcing firms from filing new applications under the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, according to The Times of India.The contrast highlights the challenge facing the US as it seeks to meet growing demand for skilled workers while prioritising domestic hiring.The report, backed by Jobs for the Future (JFF) and the Burning Glass Institute (BGI), says the US workforce system is preparing only 55 qualified workers for every 100 needed across key technical fields.It estimates that 24% of the skilled trades workforce is aged 55 or older, raising concerns about retirements and replacement needs. Demand is also growing amid investments in data centres, energy modernisation and advanced manufacturing.Industrial machinery mechanics and millwrights rank at the 98th percentile on the national Labour Shortage Index, while electricians rank at the 85th percentile.The report points to a widening gap between the number of skilled workers required and the workforce being prepared to meet that demand.PERM suspension affects major technology firmsThe US department of labour suspended eight technology and outsourcing firms from filing new PERM applications. The affected companies include Indian IT firms Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech and Cognizant, as well as US companies Microsoft and Adobe.PERM is a key step in the employment-based green card process for many foreign workers, including some H-1B visa holders. The reported suspension has added uncertainty for Indian IT professionals seeking permanent residency through employer sponsorship.US officials cited concerns about wage undercutting and alleged misuse of foreign-worker programmes. The administration has said its aim is to encourage companies to hire American workers.A test for US workforce policyThe two developments present a challenge for US workforce policy. The skilled-trades report points to a substantial shortfall in the domestic pipeline, while the immigration crackdown seeks to reduce reliance on foreign workers.Whether domestic training and recruitment can meet the projected demand of 1.7 million new skilled workers a year through 2035 remains a key question.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1956, a 60-year-old California woman found building blocks too expensive and began hauling bottles from a dump; 25 years later she had turned tens of thousands of discarded objects into a 15-building folk-art village
articles.summary: When Tressa Prisbrey was 60 years old, she wanted to build a small shed for her large pencil collection.
articles.body: When Tressa Prisbrey was 60 years old, she wanted to build a small shed for her large pencil collection. In 1956, she found that concrete blocks cost more than she could afford. Rather than give up, the California resident began collecting thousands of discarded glass bottles and household items from a nearby landfill. Over the next 25 years, she turned a one-third-acre lot in Simi Valley into Bottle Village, a well-known folk-art site with 15 structures, shrines, mosaic paths and sculpture gardens. According to historical records kept by Preserve Bottle Village, the non-profit organisation that looks after the site, the project began soon after Prisbrey and her husband parked their trailer on Cochran Street. After buying the land, she had little money left for building materials, so she turned to a local dump to find glass bottles.Constructing structures out of landfill scrapsSoda bottles usually had a two-cent deposit, so people rarely threw them away. Prisbrey instead collected discarded milk of magnesia bottles, alcohol bottles and other glass containers. She mixed mortar by hand and placed the bottles horizontally in the walls, with their bases facing outwards. The glass allowed natural light to pass through, creating colourful patterns inside the structures. From 1956 to the mid-1960s, Prisbrey built 15 separate structures, each with a single room. Official site records show that three were called Pencil Houses, where she displayed thousands of pencils. Other buildings included the Doll House, which held more than 600 dolls she had rescued from being thrown away. Once she ran out of space to build more structures, Prisbrey began decorating almost every available part of the property. She made mosaic paths from broken tiles and crockery, created a headlight garden from old car parts, and built shrines using seashells, horseshoes and discarded household items.Art born from grief and showmanshipFolk-art experts and art historians see Bottle Village as both a personal memorial and a remarkable creative achievement. Prisbrey outlived six of her seven children, and she built several parts of the site to remember family members she had lost. Records published by Preserve Bottle Village explain how her personal experiences shaped specific structures. She built the Shell House in just two days after learning that one of her sons was critically ill. The Heart-shaped Shrine was dedicated to her daughter Velma. Although many of the structures were linked to painful events, Prisbrey brought humour and a natural flair for entertaining visitors to her work. As news of the unusual site spread, Bottle Village became a popular local attraction. Prisbrey led daily walking tours and charged visitors admission fees ranging from 25 cents to one dollar. When people asked about her methods and how she worked without standard building materials, Prisbrey gave a straightforward answer. She believed creativity mattered more than money. "Anyone can do something with a million dollars. Look at Disney. But it takes more than money to make something out of nothing and look at the fun I have doing it," Prisbrey remarked in statements recorded in the project archives.Critical acclaim and historical preservationPrisbrey never considered herself a professional artist, but her work gained wider attention in the art world during the 1970s. In 1974, architectural critic Esther McCoy discussed the site's cultural importance in an essay for a catalogue published by the Walker Art Centre in Minnesota. "At the root of her uniqueness is a divine disorder; she has a passion for all discarded objects and shows a willingness to provide them all, equally, a place in her scheme," McCoy wrote in her analysis of Prisbrey's work. Bottle Village received official recognition in 1981, when it was named California State Historical Landmark No. 939. It was later designated a Ventura County Cultural Landmark and a Simi Valley City Landmark. In 1996, it was added to the National Register of Historic Places. Prisbrey moved to San Francisco in 1982 because of her declining health. She died in 1988 at the age of 92. Ownership of Bottle Village had been transferred to Preserve Bottle Village in 1986. The site received further recognition in 2025, when it became an affiliate member of Historic Artists' Homes and Studios. The national programme is managed by the National Trust for Historic Preservation and recognises places connected to artists and their work.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: ‘Jatayu’ returns to Amherst Row through Sukeas St puja theme
articles.summary: Sukeas Street Durga Puja in Kolkata honours actor Santosh Dutta’s birth centenary with a Jatayu-themed pandal recreating scenes from Satyajit Ray films.
articles.body: Kolkata: On Sukeas Street, a neighbourhood puja working within modest means but competing fiercely in imagination, has turned nostalgia into its strongest material. Its theme this year is Santosh Dutta, the actor whose comic timing, expressive face and unmistakably Bengali mannerisms made him one of the most-loved figures in Bengali cinema.The tribute comes on Dutta’s birth centenary. Born on Dec 2, 1925, in undivided Bengal, he came to live in the neighbourhood, at 49, Amherst Row, when he was seven. Known as Suradhwani Kutir, the house remained his address for life. For organisers, that local connection makes the tribute intimate rather than ceremonial.“For many in the neighbourhood, Dutta is not just a cinema artiste but a resident who used to walk the streets and have tea at local stalls. In life, his persona was very different from that on screen: he was serious and rarely cracked jokes,” recounted Sibendu Mitra.The pandal treats the theme like a walk through Bengali memory. Using sculpture, painted frames, light, shadow and installations, it recreates moments from Dutta’s life and screen presence. Old Kolkata lanes, a theatre stage and the suggestion of a film set appear in layers, allowing visitors to move through spaces that evoke both the city and the cinema that shaped him.Dutta’s association with Satyajit Ray forms the installation’s emotional centre. Ray brought him from theatre to cinema, and the pandal marks that turning point through ‘Parash Pathar’, his debut film. From there, it invokes ‘Teen Kanya’, ‘Mahapurush’, ‘Goopy Gyne Bagha Byne’, ‘Sonar Kella’, ‘Jana Aranya’, ‘Joi Baba Felunath’ and ‘Hirak Rajar Deshe’ through character studies, symbolic props and stylised tableaux.A key attraction is Lalmohan Ganguly, or Jatayu, the thriller writer from ‘Sonar Kella’ and ‘Joi Baba Felunath’. Dutta made Jatayu more than comic relief, giving him warmth, fear, vanity, innocence and loyalty.“I have drawn heavily from ‘Joi Baba Felunath’ and the character Lalmohan Babu who uses the ‘chadmanaam’ or pen name of Jatayu. We have tried to recreate the Ghoshal family house thakurdalan showcased in the movie. Since space is limited, we have used the balconies of the Srimani Bari as part of the thakurdalan installation,” explained artist Indrajit Ray, adding that a golden Ganesh has been kept inside the lion’s jaw just like in the film. The Idol-maker Bablu Paul was asked to make the idol resemble those seen in bonedi baris in the 1970s. The tribute also recalls Dutta’s “Researcher” in ‘Hirak Rajar Deshe’, Abalakanta from ‘Ogo Bodhu Sundari’, and his association with Gopal Bhar. Together, they underline his place in Bengali wit, folk humour and satire.The Sukeas Street puja refuses to treat comedy as lesser art. It presents Dutta’s humour as observation, rhythm and emotional truth. Dutta, who died on March 5, 1988, returns here as a cherished “Parash Pathar” — a touchstone of laughter, mystery and memory.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Kolkata | Silver Rate in Kolkata | Bank Holidays in Kolkata | Public Holidays in Kolkata | Kolkata AQI | Weather in Kolkata | Petrol Price in Kolkata | Diesel Price in Kolkata | CNG Price in Kolkata | LPG Price in KolkataStay updated with the latest Kolkata news. articles.title: ​A New Zealand couple bought an abandoned school, then spent three years and about NZ$250,000 turning the classroom into a home and chalet; the property is now listed for enquiries over NZ$595,000
articles.summary: For years, an old school sat quietly on the edge of Tokanui, a small township in Southland. Then Ian ‘Hippy’ Rogers and his wife, Sue, arrived.
articles.body: For years, an old school sat quietly on the edge of Tokanui, a small township in Southland. Then Ian ‘Hippy’ Rogers and his wife, Sue, arrived. They took one look at the school and saw something most people didn’t. The couple knew the neglected property had the potential to become a home.The school at Quarry Hill first opened in the late 1800s, although the building the couple bought dated from 1958. It closed in 1993, and subsequent owners had done little with the property.In 2017, when the couple arrived, hedges had swallowed much of the site. But they weren’t ready to give up. They invested a couple of years in turning the school into a home. Now, the property is on the market for enquiries over NZ$595,000, according to a report by Trade Me Property.Two ways of looking at a ruinWhen the couple first laid eyes on the dilapidated building, they saw two things. Sue saw what it could become, while Ian saw the work it would take. Sue admits the decision required some persuasion.“I wouldn’t say we agreed instantly. It was more a wife nagging,” Sue told the outlet.Ian laughs when he remembers it. “She was looking at it, going, ‘This will be wonderful’, and I was looking at it, going, ‘Look at the work involved’.”Before they knew it, they were looking at a long-abandoned schoolhouse, a derelict outdoor swimming pool and changing rooms that were almost swallowed by the hedges.Sue had always wanted to renovate a school, although she admits people look at her strangely when they discover her day job. She’s a school principal. “We’d been looking for something unusual. We liked renovating, so my random idea was to find an old school in Southland.”Renovation beginsBefore any walls could be touched, the couple had to clear the land. Thirty years of hedges, weeds and wildlife had taken over the half-hectare block. They worked with Invercargill builder Craig Brown, and the school was stripped back to its framing. New insulation was installed, and most of the windows were retrofitted with double glazing. Luckily, the building’s structure was in good condition. “Structurally, it was already about 90 to 95% sound,” Ian said.A new 9.6-metre beam was installed above the kitchen and lounge to support part of the rear wall and a small extension. They reused original materials wherever possible.A school that still feels like oneSue wanted the house to retain its past. “It had to feel like a fun school,” she said. She chose the colour palette, giving the school a bold and quirky look. “It’s still got the character and the history of the school within the building.”Some original details survived the renovation. For instance, a giant chalkboard hangs above the bed, and the cubby holes where generations of students once left their school bags are still there.Pool turns into chaletAnother part of the renovation was the pool, which was badly damaged when the couple bought the property. It had to go. “It could have become a nursery, a big glasshouse or a veggie garden,” Sue added. But they kept coming back to a beach-themed chalet that could serve as short-term accommodation. The main building took about three years to finish. The one-bedroom retreat inside the former pool came later.The renovations cost the couple an estimated NZ$250,000. That figure excludes their own labour and is slightly higher than Sue’s initial estimate.The property is now listed for enquiries over NZ$595,000 through JJ Morgan at Bayleys. The couple is ready for their next project, and Sue already knows what she doesn’t want. “Not an old school!” For now, she is done with schools.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.summary: Over 100 detained near Jantar Mantar as SFI-DYFI and Youth Congress march, target CEC Gyanesh Kumar, and oppose protest-site denotification and voter roll issues.
articles.body: New Delhi: Over 100 people were detained near Jantar Mantar Tuesday after student and youth outfits held two separate marches towards the iconic site.Both demonstrations echoed similar slogans, including “Jantar Mantar wapas karo” and “Gyanesh Kumar isteefa do”.
