articles.title: Israel’s former security chief sues Netanyahu for October 7 defamation
articles.summary: Bar and Netanyahu have traded blame over the Hamas-led attack, as elections in Israel loom.
articles.body:
The former head of Israel’s domestic security agency Shin Bet has sued Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for defamation over claims of his responsibility in the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack.

Coming just before Israel’s close-fought October 27 election in which Netanyahu is fighting for his political life, the case filed on Wednesday is set to ramp up the country’s political drama.

Ronen Bar, the former director of Shin Bet, accused Netanyahu of “lying to cover himself” and said it was slanderous of the prime minister to have accused him of “criminal failures” over the attack, in a 134-page court document.

Bar said he telephoned the prime minister’s military secretary as soon as signs of a possible attack became apparent, but that he did not have Netanyahu’s direct number.

Netanyahu has said he was not alerted by Bar on the morning of the Hamas-led assault, insisting that he could have stopped the attack had the Shin Bet’s then-director or military leaders called to wake him up the day of the early-morning attack.

Bar’s lawsuit says Netanyahu made accusations “that he knew to be false, with the aim of diverting the debate from his own responsibility for the events of October 7”.

Instead, it was Netanyahu’s policies over several years that had “increased the dangers posed by terrorist organisations in Gaza”, it said.

On Wednesday, Netanyahu responded to Bar’s accusations in a statement issued by his Likud party saying, “Ronen, are you serious?”

“You had my number on the red line and could have called me immediately, as all security chiefs do,” Netanyahu asked, adding, “How many lives could we have saved if only you had called in time?”

Bar resigned as head of Shin Bet in June 2025 amid recriminations over the deadliest attack in Israel’s history, while insisting he had informed Netanyahu of the threat in advance.

He is seeking three million shekels (about $968,500) in damages from Netanyahu.

The allegations in Bar’s lawsuit come days after Netanyahu’s former military secretary, Avi Gil, told Israel’s Channel 12 that the prime minister’s office had “falsified records related to October 7, 2023”, including altering the recorded time of a key phone call.

Gil, who served as Netanyahu’s military secretary from July 2021 to May 2024, said a stenographer in the prime minister’s office approached him in January 2024 with instructions from Netanyahu’s chief of staff to change the time of a four-minute call from 6:40am local time (03:40GMT) to 6:29am (03:29 GMT).

“She told me, I’m not allowed to change it,” said Gil, accusing the head of Netanyahu’s office of manipulating telephone records, adding, “Those are facts, and there is no dispute about them.”

Last month, the Wall Street Journal reported that Netanyahu had been warned of the attack by Egypt’s intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel.

In a rare move, Kamel reportedly phoned the prime minister just days before the attack, underscoring previous warnings in September 2023, when he is said to have flown to Israel to warn security officials in person that Hamas was planning an attack.

Polls show Netanyahu is in a tight race to stay in power in the October 27 election, after being hammered by former staff and government officials as well as the opposition for failing to prevent the bloodshed.

At least 1,221 Israelis were killed on October 7, 2023, after Hamas broke through the fence separating Israel and Gaza, according to Israeli official figures.

Also, 251 Israelis were taken captive, including the bodies of 44 Israelis killed that day.

In the three years since, Israel has killed more than 74,300 people in Gaza, according to the Health Ministry in the enclave.

More than 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed in Israeli attacks since a tentative “ceasefire” backed by the US was reached last year.

articles.body:
Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas) on Wednesday expressed his support for President Trump’s recent push for an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, but he also slammed Russian President Vladimir Putin over Russia’s apparent betrayal of the claimed ceasefire.

“President Trump did the right thing by trying to force an energy ceasefire. You have to *try*. But unfortunately a deal depends on the parties involved – and Putin is a backstabbing liar,” Crenshaw said in a Wednesday post on the social platform X .

“Putin should not get away with trying to embarrass our President. He should regret it,” the Texas Republican added. “Apply the sanctions under the full force of the new law. Enable Ukrainian drones to bomb the HELL out of Russian infrastructure. It’s time. It costs us NOTHING.”

On Sunday, Trump claimed an energy ceasefire deal had come together between Russia and Ukraine, only a few days after his administration unveiled a deal to acquire diesel from Russia while lifting sanctions.

“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump said on Truth Social at the time. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!”

Later Sunday, Russia struck a power plant in eastern Ukraine , contradicting Trump’s earlier announcement.

ABC News reported over the weekend, citing a local official, that a power plant in the city of Kharkiv had been struck twice. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the strikes, alongside others.

“Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day today. There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening,” Zelensky said Sunday on X.

Zelensky did not appear to be aware of Trump’s claim of an energy ceasefire after he announced it, saying to Axios that the deal “was news for me.”

“But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree,” he added.

articles.title: Contraceptive coil 'helped uncover my ovarian cancer'
articles.summary: Caroline Bailey was diagnosed after suffering with "a stabbing pain in the middle of my abdomen".
articles.body:
When Caroline Bailey was suffering with sharp, stabbing pains in her stomach, she thought it was being caused by her contraceptive coil.

In severe pain, the 54-year-old went to her GP, desperate to have it removed, only for scans to reveal it was in fact a 13cm (5in) tumour pressing against her coil .

She was diagnosed with stage three ovarian cancer in June 2023 and feared she might not live for another two years.

Now, with no evidence of disease after chemotherapy and surgery, she said: "I absolutely think that the coil saved my life, which is mad."

She had been experiencing severe abdominal pain since March and thought the coil was to blame.

"I started to have the worst stomach pains – like a stabbing pain in the middle of my abdomen," she said.

"So, I kept going back into the doctors and said, 'I think the coil needs to come out'."

Caroline, from Trelogan, Flintshire, said she was referred to a sexual health clinic as there were no appointments available, but staff there could not remove it.

With her pain getting worse, she "crawled into the doctors on my hands and knees" in May, asking for the coil to be removed.

"I wanted to rip it out myself, but you can't. I thought it was killing me."

"I was going to the doctor, saying, 'This coil is stabbing me', and I just hate how long it took for me to be taken seriously.

"I wish it was easier for women to get diagnosed."

Caroline was diagnosed with endometriosis – where cells similar to those in the lining of the womb grow in other parts of the body – in her mid 20s.

But, with "no history of ovarian cancer in the family whatsoever" so thought her pain was being caused by her coil.

Caroline said she was given a CA125 blood test form, which is used to check the level of the CA125 protein in the blood and can support a diagnosis of ovarian cancer, as her doctor wanted to see if that was causing the problems.

She was given this form as, although she believed it was the coil causing her pain, a doctor wanted to check for ovarian cancer due to her symptoms.

She took a blood test that can support a diagnosis of ovarian cancer that returned a reading of proteins of 72 units per ml (U/ml).

According to charity Ovarian Cancer Action, women over 40 should be referred for further investigations if it is over 35 U/ml.

Caroline was put on a two-week pathway, which she described as being "in this crazy world of, oh my God".

Subsequent scans revealed the tumour and a biopsy confirmed the cancer was stage three and it had spread to the omentum – a large piece of fatty tissue that lies near to the womb and ovaries.

What are the symptoms of ovarian cancer?

The NHS lists the main symptoms of ovarian cancer as frequently - approximately 12 or more times a month - having:

Pain or tenderness in the tummy or the area between your hips

No appetite or feeling full quickly after eating

An urgent need to wee or needing to wee more often

"I couldn't believe the size of it. I actually thought, 'I won't live for another two years'," Caroline said.

She started chemotherapy soon after and had four rounds of treatment at The Christie in Manchester, which shrank her tumour to 8cm (3in).

On October 26, she had a total hysterectomy - where the womb and cervix are removed - along with the removal of her omentum and appendix during a six-hour operation.

The surgery means Caroline now has no evidence of disease, but she was told ovarian cancer can be "unpredictable" with a high re-occurrence rate.

One month after her surgery, Caroline's grandson Roman was born, and she underwent two further rounds of chemotherapy in January 2024, along with follow-up CT scans.

As part of the testing, it was revealed that she had gene mutations that increased her risk of breast and ovarian cancer.

Caroline is now having consultations about a double mastectomy to remove both breasts, along with reconstruction surgery and implants, as part of a trial, and her family members are being genetically tested.

"But the best thing about this, about having ovarian cancer, is my girls know what they're dealing with and they can have preventative surgery," she said.

"My diagnosis makes me live for now... and what I know now is, tomorrow is definitely not guaranteed."

Caroline moved house several times during her treatment, got divorced and lost her job - even living out of her car - and said money was her "biggest worry".

She now wants to encourage other women to get any unusual symptoms checked and to advocate for themselves.

"I've definitely had to change my life because I had cancer," she said.

"My motto is: Be healthy, be happy, be kind."

Cancer Research UK said ovarian cancer was the 16th most common cancer, with about 7,700 new cases every year.

In July 2026, 51.3% of women started their first definitive treatment within 62 days of first being suspected of having gynaecological cancer - well below the target of 75% - according to Welsh government data.
